evidence.title: Byblos (Jbeil, Lebanon): Cedar timber harbor & Old Kingdom Egypt maritime link
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified Early Bronze–Late Bronze temple offerings naming Egyptian pharaohs alongside petrography of imported Levantine Combed Ware jars in Giza.
evidence.summary: Mounted maritime timber, pine resin, and oil convoys ("Byblos ships") between the Lebanese coast and Old Kingdom Nile deltas from the third millennium BCE, seeding early alphabetic script development.
evidence.limits: Harbor wharves are partially overlaid by modern coastal masonry.

evidence.title: Knossos & Kommos (Crete): Minoan palace-ports & Egyptian-Levantine exchange
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated shipsheds at southern harbour Kommos, Egyptian stone vessels, Cypriot pottery, and Linear A/B accounting tablets.
evidence.summary: Connected Aegean island mariners to Nile and Levantine courts, exchanging silver, olive oil, and woolen textiles for Nilotic gold, alabaster, ostrich eggs, and eastern tin.
evidence.limits: Linear A administrative records remain undeciphered.

evidence.title: Akrotiri (Thera / Santorini): Cycladic Bronze Age maritime town
evidence.dateBasis: Tephra-sealed multi-story ashlar houses preserving miniature ship frescoes, imported African-motif wall art, and standardized lead weights.
evidence.summary: Volcanic ash preserved a thriving Bronze Age Aegean harbor city displaying ship processions, copper balance weights, and exotic Nile-world artistic exchanges.
evidence.limits: Absence of human skeletons indicates inhabitants evacuated prior to the final eruption.

evidence.title: Ugarit & Minet el-Beida (Ras Shamra, Syria): Polyglot Late Bronze emporium
evidence.dateBasis: Royal palace archives in Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet, Akkadian diplomatic correspondence, and port warehouses at Minet el-Beida.
evidence.summary: Cosmopolitan Syrian port linking Mycenaean, Cypriot, Hittite, and Egyptian merchants with overland Euphrates routes until sudden urban destruction around 1185 BCE.
evidence.limits: Harbor warehouses represent the final Late Bronze horizon.

evidence.title: Enkomi & Hala Sultan Tekke (Cyprus / Alashiya): Oxhide copper hubs
evidence.dateBasis: Slag workshops, oxhide ingot molds, Amarna diplomatic tablets from Alashiya, and lagoon harbor excavations at Hala Sultan Tekke.
evidence.summary: Island crossroads anchoring eastern Mediterranean copper metallurgy—casting Troodos ore into standardized 29-kilogram oxhide ingots shipped to Egypt, Syria, Greece, and Sardinia.
evidence.limits: Trace-element recycling complicates single-mine provenance on late Bronze objects.

evidence.title: Uluburun Shipwreck (Kaş, SW Turkey): c. 1320 BCE Late Bronze royal cargo
evidence.dateBasis: Deep underwater excavation yielding 10 tons of Cypriot copper ingots, 1 ton Central Asian/Anatolian tin, 175 cobalt glass ingots, terebinth resin, ebony, ivory, and Nefertiti’s gold scarab.
evidence.summary: The single richest sealed time capsule of Late Bronze Mediterranean trade, uniting raw tin from Central Asian mountains, Cypriot copper, Egyptian gold/glass, African blackwood/ivory, and Aegean weapons in one 15-metre Syrian cedar hull.
evidence.limits: Represents a high-value elite palace consignment supplemented by small-scale merchant goods.

evidence.title: Tyre & Sidon (Phoenicia, Lebanon): Purple dye, cedar & maritime expansion
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified Phoenician harbor sequences, imported Greek drinking wares at Tell el-Burak, and westward amphora typologies.
evidence.summary: Pioneered Iron Age long-distance shipping from the Levant to Tunisia (Carthage), Sicily, Sardinia, and Atlantic Iberia, diffusing the 22-letter Phoenician alphabet alongside Tyrian purple textiles and silver.
evidence.limits: Hellenistic, Roman, and modern Tyre overlay early Iron Age residential quarters.

evidence.title: Gadir / Cádiz (SW Spain): Phoenician Atlantic–Mediterranean silver & tin port
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon dates from Teatro Cómico stratified layers alongside underwater La Caleta maritime votive assemblages and Punic fish-salting vats.
evidence.summary: Westernmost Phoenician foundation linking Atlantic tin/Tartessian silver mining with Mediterranean Garum fish-sauce amphora distribution across Carthage and Greece.
evidence.limits: Urban density across Cádiz restricts horizontal exposure of early ninth-century strata.

evidence.title: Naukratis & Thonis-Heracleion (Nile Delta, Egypt): Greek–Egyptian emporia
evidence.dateBasis: Saitic–Ptolemaic customs decrees, bilingual stelae, underwater temple wrecks in Aboukir Bay, and thousands of Aegean trade amphorae.
evidence.summary: Regulated Egypt’s Mediterranean maritime gateway under the Saite 26th Dynasty and Ptolemies, channeling Greek silver coinage and wine in exchange for Nile wheat, natron, and papyrus.
evidence.limits: Canopic channel subsidence submerged Thonis-Heracleion beneath shallow bay waters.

evidence.title: Cyrene & Apollonia Harbor (Cyrenaica, Libya): Greek North African grain & silphium port
evidence.dateBasis: Theraean foundation decree inscriptions, coin dies depicting prized silphium plants, and submerged quay ruins at Apollonia.
evidence.summary: Founded by Aegean settlers on the Green Mountain escarpment of Libya, Cyrene exported barley, horses, and prized medicinal silphium across Greek and Roman networks.
evidence.limits: Apollonia waterfront subsidence affects earliest Archaic harbor phases.

evidence.title: Corinth & the Diolkos Trackway (Greece): Isthmus haulage & trans-Med commerce
evidence.dateBasis: Paved limestone trackway grooves across the Isthmus paired with excavated Punic transport amphorae and Corinthian pottery.
evidence.summary: Pioneered the Diolkos paved overland portage hauling cargoes and small vessels between Aegean and Ionian seas, with excavations revealing salted-fish amphorae shipped directly from Carthaginian North Africa.
evidence.limits: Construction of the modern Corinth Canal cut segments of the ancient paved road.

evidence.title: Massalia (Marseille) & Emporion: Phocaean Greek Western ports
evidence.dateBasis: Ancient Old Port quay timbers, Greek/Celtic/Etruscan shipwreck cargoes near Marseille, and native wine-amphora kilns.
evidence.summary: Established at the Rhône River mouth around 600 BCE, Massalia introduced commercial viticulture, Greek coinage, and Rhône-Valley trade tying Gaulish societies into Mediterranean shipping.
evidence.limits: Harbor dredging reveals discontinuous Archaic vs. Hellenistic quay phases.

evidence.title: Piraeus & Athens (Attica, Greece): Trireme ship-sheds & Black Sea grain lifeline
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated stone Zea & Munychia trireme ship-sheds, maritime grain laws (sigon), and Laurion silver tetradrachm circulation.
evidence.summary: Athenian naval hegemony rested on Piraeus’ triple fortified harbors, Laurion silver coinage, and legally protected sea convoys importing grain from Crimea, Egypt, and Sicily.
evidence.limits: Dense modern port redevelopment limits interior access to Kantharos commercial docks.

evidence.title: Syracuse (Sicily): Central Mediterranean twin-harbor crossroads
evidence.dateBasis: Ortygia stratigraphic foundations, Great Harbor siege archaeology, and Sicilian-Punic coin and amphora sequences.
evidence.summary: Guarding the central bottleneck between Italy, Tunisia, and the Aegean, Syracuse became one of the classical Mediterranean’s wealthiest naval powers and a pivotal wheat basket.
evidence.limits: Continuously occupied island of Ortygia limits wide-area Classical street clearance.

evidence.title: Alexandria & the Pharos Lighthouse (Egypt): Hellenistic megacity & annona hub
evidence.dateBasis: Submerged Eastern Harbour Heptastadion & Pharos masonry blocks paired with Egyptian-Roman grain-fleet papyri.
evidence.summary: Designed with twin artificial harbors around Pharos Island, Alexandria unified Red Sea Indian Ocean spices, Egyptian grain fleets, papyrus workshops, and cosmopolitan scientific libraries under Ptolemaic, Roman, and Byzantine rule.
evidence.limits: Seismic subsidence and urban overlay restrict land excavations outside underwater harbour surveys.

population.note: Late Ptolemaic Alexandria scholarly range (accounting for Diodorus’s free-citizen count plus unenumerated households)

evidence.title: Rhodes (Aegean): Hellenistic wine-amphora standardization & maritime sea law
evidence.dateBasis: Over 100,000 stamped Rhodian transport amphora handles recovered from Alexandria to Carthage and the Black Sea.
evidence.summary: Standardized amphora capacity stamps and maritime commercial rules (later remembered as Rhodian Sea Law) made Rhodes the premier Hellenistic banking and carrying trade republic.
evidence.limits: Dated amphora-stamp chronologies continue to undergo refinement by magistracy sequences.

evidence.title: Delos (Cyclades, Aegean): Hellenistic–Roman duty-free entrepôt
evidence.dateBasis: Merchant guild agoras (Poseidoniasts of Berytus), polyglot dedications, warehouse piers, and epigraphic trade records.
evidence.summary: Declared a tax-exempt Roman free harbor in 166 BCE, tiny rocky Delos concentrated Egyptian, Syrian, Italian, and Greek trading guilds alongside brutal mass enslavement markets before Mithridatic raids destroyed the city.
evidence.limits: Enslaved people’s residential spaces leave subtle traces relative to monumental merchant courtyards.

evidence.title: Ostia & Imperial Portus (Tiber mouth, Italy): Megaharbors of Imperial Rome
evidence.dateLabel: c. 300 BCE–550 CE (Claudian basin 42 CE; Trajan hexagon 112 CE)
evidence.dateBasis: Massive hydraulic-concrete outer breakwaters, Trajan’s 32-hectare hexagonal inner basin, horrea granaries, and isotopic cemetery bioarchaeology.
evidence.summary: Engineered to dock massive African and Alexandrian grain freighters (annona), Portus sustained Rome’s million-person metropolis with docked granaries, marble yards, and immigrant merchant quarters.
evidence.limits: Coastal progradation shifted modern shorelines kilometres seaward of imperial docks.

evidence.title: Caesarea Maritima (Sebastos Harbor, Levant): Hydraulic concrete engineering
evidence.dateBasis: Cores of submerged breakwaters revealing imported Campanian pozzolanic volcanic ash mixed with lime mortar that set underwater.
evidence.summary: Constructed on a harborless sandy coast with huge caissons of volcanic-ash Roman hydraulic concrete, Sebastos became a major imperial Levantine hub importing Mediterranean wines and exporting Palestinian amphorae.
evidence.limits: Fault-line subsidence broke outer harbor moles into submerged rubble reef zones.

evidence.title: Hispalis / Baetica & Rome’s Monte Testaccio: Imperial olive-oil scale
evidence.dateBasis: Artificial Rome hill composed of an estimated 53 million discarded olive-oil Dressel 20 amphorae, with painted fiscal tituli picti stamps tracing Spanish Guadalquivir and North African estates.
evidence.summary: Quantifies state-organized imperial shipping scale—carrying Baetican and later Tripolitanian olive oil across specialized bulk container amphora networks to feed urban baths, lamps, and rations across the empire.
evidence.limits: Monte Testaccio ends around 260 CE as North African cylindrical amphorae (less suited to mound stacking) increasingly supplied Italy.

evidence.title: Ephesus & Miletus (Ionia, Western Anatolia): Marble avenues & Asian province ports
evidence.dateBasis: Harbor gate epigraphy, customs-tax inscription (Monumentum Ephesenum), and silting core profiles across Cayster and Maeander deltas.
evidence.summary: Terminal seafront ports of western Anatolian overland roads exporting purple cloth, ceramics, slaves, and Asian goods across Greco-Roman waters before river silt stranded their quays kilometres inland.
evidence.limits: Alluvial silting masked early Archaic Ionian waterfront structures.

evidence.title: Constantinople (Yenikapı / Theodosian Harbor): 37 Byzantine shipwrecks
evidence.dateBasis: Rescue excavations uncovering 37 waterlogged merchant galleys and round hulls alongside Ganos wine amphorae and ship timbers.
evidence.summary: Transformed Mediterranean logistics when Constantinople succeeded Rome—salvaging the Yenikapı ships reveals transition from shell-first Roman hull joinery toward faster Byzantine frame-first merchant vessels.
evidence.limits: Harbor siltation ended Yenikapı anchorage activity after the eleventh century CE.

evidence.title: Serçe Limanı ("Glass Wreck", SW Turkey): c. 1025 CE Byzantine–Fatimid ship
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated shipwreck hull loaded with 3 metric tons of broken Fatimid Syrian glass cullet/vessel scrap alongside Christian amphorae and coins.
evidence.summary: Iconic eleventh-century wreck proving vibrant everyday Christian–Muslim merchant shipping across the Byzantine–Fatimid frontier, carrying recyclable Syrian raw glass toward Constantinople workshops.
evidence.limits: Single-vessel snapshot highlighting specialized regional cabotage.

evidence.title: Al-Mahdiyya & Palermo (Tunisia–Sicily Strait): Cairo Geniza & Islamic commerce
evidence.dateBasis: Thousands of eleventh-century mercantile letters preserved in Cairo’s Ben Ezra Synagogue Geniza linking Fustat, Alexandria, Ifriqiya, and Sicily.
evidence.summary: Maghribi and Geniza merchant letters reveal dense seasonal sailing schedules exchanging Egyptian flax, eastern spices, Tunisian olive oil, and Sicilian silk—showing commercial trust networks crossing Islamic North Africa and southern Italy.
evidence.limits: Geniza documents illuminate literate Arabic-script Jewish merchant networks especially during the eleventh century CE.

evidence.title: Amalfi & Pisa (Tyrrhenian Italy): Sea codes, Islamic–Italian basins & ports
evidence.dateBasis: Tabula Amalphitana maritime law tradition, North African imported bacini ceramic bowls mounted in Pisan church facades, and consulate treaties.
evidence.summary: Early Italian maritime republics pioneered maritime partnership contracts (commenda/colleganza) while operating fondaco merchant quarters in Alexandria, Tunis, and Bougie.
evidence.limits: Silting of Porto Pisano and Genoese rivalry ended Pisa’s maritime independence after 1284.

evidence.title: Venice & the Venetian Arsenale (Adriatic Lagoon): Standardized galley convoys
evidence.dateBasis: State Arsenale shipyard architecture, muda convoy auctions to Alexandria and Beirut, and commercial port registers.
evidence.summary: Marshy Adriatic refuge turned maritime republic utilizing assembly-line shipbuilding at the Arsenale and timed state-convoy mudae connecting Mamluk Alexandria, Crete, Constantinople, and northern Europe.
evidence.limits: Ottoman and Atlantic shifts gradually eroded Venice’s eastern spice monopoly after 1500 CE.

evidence.title: Genoa (Liguria): Joint-stock maone, Casa di San Giorgio & Black Sea–Atlantic reach
evidence.dateBasis: Notarial maritime contracts preserving marine insurance premiums, bills of exchange, and Maghreb–Genoa coral/gold shipments.
evidence.summary: Genoese merchants invented marine insurance contracts, bulk alum/grain round-ships, and public-debt banks (Casa di San Giorgio), operating trading hubs from Caffa in Crimea to Ceuta and Seville.
evidence.limits: Early notarial survival skews visibility toward Genoa’s twelfth-century onward records.

evidence.title: Port Said & Suez Canal Opening (Egypt, 1869 CE): Steam link to the Indian Ocean
evidence.dateBasis: Engineering excavation records across the Isthmus of Suez (built chiefly by conscripted Egyptian corvée labor) and steamship tonnage registers.
evidence.summary: Reconnected the Mediterranean directly to the Red Sea by excavated sea-level channel in 1869, transforming Port Said, Aden, Port Sudan, and Mombasa into industrial coaling-and-steam corridors linking Europe, East Africa, and Asia.
evidence.limits: Built under unequal nineteenth-century Anglo-French financial concessions and heavy forced Egyptian labor tolls.

waves.title: Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean prestige & metal exchange (Uluburun track)
waves.summary: Counter-clockwise eastern Mediterranean currents carried royal diplomatic cargoes of Cypriot oxhide copper, Asian tin, glass ingots, ebony, and ivory connecting Syria, Cyprus, Crete, Mycenae, and New Kingdom Egypt.
waves.limits: Schematic circulation arc linking excavated wreck and palace contexts rather than one vessel track.

waves.title: Phoenician & Greek Iron Age colonization and container shipping
waves.summary: Two overlapping maritime city networks linked Tyre and Carthage with Corinth, Syracuse, Naukratis, Massalia, and Atlantic Cádiz, standardizing transport amphorae, silver coinage, and alphabetic scripts.
waves.limits: Schematic arc integrating separate Phoenician-Punic and Aegean port traditions.

waves.title: Imperial Rome grain fleets to Geniza & Italian-Maghreb sea lanes
waves.summary: Sustained bulk maritime shipping connecting Alexandria, Caesarea, Constantinople, Ifriqiya, Sicily, Rome’s Portus, and Venice/Genoa across imperial annona fleets and medieval Geniza/fondaco networks.
waves.limits: Merges millennia-scale trunk corridors; political control and dominant port hubs shifted markedly between Roman, Byzantine, Fatimid, and Italian eras.
